modules.title: Foundations
modules.description: Start with the ideas that make every structure and algorithm easier to understand.

slides.title: Structures organize; algorithms act
paragraphs: A data structure is a way to organize values and the relationships between them. A shopping list keeps items in a sequence; a map connects places by roads. An algorithm is a finite set of clear steps for doing a task, such as finding a name or arranging numbers.
Neither idea depends on a programming language. We choose a structure and an algorithm together to make a particular task understandable and efficient.
bullets: Structure: how information is arranged.
Algorithm: the steps applied to that information.
Correctness and cost both matter.

slides.title: Inputs, outputs and correctness
paragraphs: An input is the information a task receives. An output is the result it promises. For “find the largest value,” [3, 8, 2] is an input and 8 is the output. The number 8 is not the input size: the size is three elements.

Correctness means meeting the promised result for every allowed input, not just one example. State preconditions (what must already be true) and define edge cases: an empty input has no largest value, so the task must explicitly return “none” or reject it.
bullets: A precondition might be “the input is sorted.”
An invariant is a fact preserved while steps repeat.
Check empty, one-element, duplicate and missing-result cases.

slides.title: Describe steps before choosing syntax
paragraphs: Pseudocode is a plain-language description of an algorithm. It uses ideas like “for each value” and “if” without requiring a particular language. To find a largest value: reject an empty sequence; remember the first value; inspect each remaining value; replace the remembered value when a larger one appears; return it.

After each inspected value, the remembered value is the largest in the inspected prefix. That invariant explains why the final answer is correct. A loop repeats a step; a condition chooses whether to perform an action.
bullets: INPUT: a nonempty sequence
best ← first value
FOR each remaining value: IF value > best THEN best ← value
OUTPUT: best

slides.title: Elements, indices, values and memory
paragraphs: An element is one item in a collection. Its value is the data stored there. An index is its position: with zero-based indices, the first position is 0 and the last is n − 1. In [8, 3, 8], index 1 contains value 3; the value 8 occurs at two different positions.

Memory can be pictured as numbered storage locations. A fixed-size contiguous array reserves neighboring slots of equal size. Our addresses are illustrative, not browser addresses. Python lists and JavaScript arrays are language abstractions and should not be assumed to have this exact layout.

slides.title: Count work as the input grows
paragraphs: Choose a basic operation before counting: for a scan, count values inspected; for a sort, count comparisons or writes. Scanning n values once performs n inspections, even if the values themselves are large. The input size n describes how much information there is, not its largest numeric value.

The same operation count can animate at different speeds. Animation duration is not an algorithm’s time complexity. Different computers also take different times for the same count. Use counts to compare growth under the same definition of work.

slides.title: Time and auxiliary space
paragraphs: Time complexity describes how work grows with input size. Auxiliary space is extra temporary storage beyond the given input and required output. Reading one array slot needs a constant amount of extra storage; copying n elements into a temporary array needs space proportional to n.

Input storage, output storage and auxiliary storage are different categories. A recursive call stack is auxiliary storage too, even if the code never explicitly allocates an array. State which space convention you are using.
bullets: O(1) auxiliary space: a fixed number of variables.
O(n) auxiliary space: one extra slot for each input element.
Counting operations does not count seconds.

slides.title: Big O, Big Omega and Big Theta
paragraphs: Asymptotic notation describes growth for sufficiently large input sizes, allowing constant factors and a finite starting region to be ignored. Big O is an upper growth bound; Big Omega (Ω) is a lower growth bound; Big Theta (Θ) is a matching upper and lower growth bound.

For 3n + 2 steps, Θ(n) is a tight description: beyond small n, the count stays between constant multiples of n. O(n²) is also an upper bound, but a loose one. A bound is about a chosen cost function; it is not automatically a best-case or worst-case claim.
bullets: Upper bound: the cost eventually grows no faster than a constant multiple.
Lower bound: the cost eventually grows at least as fast as a constant multiple.
Tight bound: both statements hold for the same growth rate.

slides.title: Common growth rates
paragraphs: Constant work, O(1), does not grow with n, such as reading a known array index. Logarithmic work, O(log n), repeatedly halves a remaining range: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 is four halvings. The base of a logarithm changes only a constant factor.

A complete scan is Θ(n). Dividing and merging across logarithmically many levels often gives Θ(n log n). Comparing every pair can be Θ(n²). Trying two choices at each of n positions creates 2ⁿ possibilities. Listing every ordering has n! possibilities (n × (n−1) × … × 1). These are growth patterns, not guarantees that a named algorithm always has that cost.

slides.title: Cases and bounds answer different questions
paragraphs: Best, average and worst cases describe which inputs of the same size we consider. Linear search has a best case when the target is first: one comparison. Its worst case is a missing target or a match at the end: n comparisons. An average-case claim needs a stated input distribution, such as equally likely matching positions.

Asymptotic bounds then describe the cost of the chosen case. The best-case cost above is Θ(1), and the worst-case cost is Θ(n). Big O does not mean “worst case,” and Big Omega does not mean “best case.” Either bound can describe a best-, average- or worst-case cost function.
bullets: Case: which input situations are considered?
Bound: how does that situation’s cost grow?
Average is not automatically halfway between best and worst.

slides.title: Analyze loops by counting repetitions
paragraphs: A loop visiting indices 0 through n−1 runs n times. Two such loops one after another run 2n times, which is Θ(n), not Θ(n²). A loop that repeatedly halves a positive counter runs about log₂ n times.

For nested loops, count the inner work for every outer iteration. If both independent loops run n times, there are n × n visits. If the inner loop runs i times on outer iteration i, add 0 + 1 + … + (n−1) = n(n−1)/2, still Θ(n²). Not every nested loop is quadratic; its limits decide.

slides.title: Recursion uses a call stack
paragraphs: A recursive function solves a task by calling itself on a smaller task. It needs a base case that stops and a rule that moves toward that base case. Countdown(n) returns immediately for n = 0; otherwise it calls countdown(n−1) and then returns.

For n = 4, calls 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 can all be active at once. Each call remembers where to return. This simple countdown takes Θ(n) time and Θ(n) call-stack space; n + 1 frames still grow linearly. Do not assume a language removes these frames automatically.

faqs.question: Does “O” stand for the worst case?
faqs.answer: No. O is an upper growth bound on the cost function you chose. First say whether you mean a best-, average- or worst-case cost, then state its bound.

faqs.question: Is a larger value a larger input?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Searching [1000] has one element; searching [1, 2, 3] has three. Here n is the number of elements. Some other tasks measure input size in bits or characters, so define it.

faqs.question: Are all nested loops O(n²)?
faqs.answer: No. Count how often each loop runs. An outer loop of n repetitions with an inner loop of three repetitions takes 3n steps, or Θ(n).

faqs.question: Does short recursive code use constant space?
faqs.answer: No. Each unfinished call can require a frame. The maximum number of simultaneously active calls determines call-stack space.

modules.title: Arrays
modules.description: Understand indexed storage, shifting, length and capacity.

slides.title: An array is a row of indexed slots
paragraphs: An array keeps values in an ordered row. Each slot holds one element, and its index tells us which slot to use. Repeated values are allowed. The first element is at index 0; if there are n elements, the last is at index n−1.

Here we illustrate fixed-size contiguous storage: equal-size slots placed next to one another. Python lists and JavaScript arrays provide related sequence operations but do not promise this identical memory layout.

slides.title: Addresses, length and capacity
paragraphs: For a contiguous array, address(i) = base_address + i × element_size. With illustrative base 1000 and four bytes per element, index 2 starts at 1008. These addresses are a teaching model, not actual browser memory.

Logical length is the number of occupied elements; capacity is the number of reserved slots. With length 3 and capacity 5, only indices 0, 1 and 2 are valid for reading. Inserting can use a spare slot, but a full fixed-capacity array must reject insertion or allocate a larger array.

slides.title: Create an initial sequence
paragraphs: Choose the initial occupied values in order. Creating [3, 1, 4] gives logical length three; creating an empty sequence gives length zero. A bounded representation also has a capacity, which limits later insertion.
Initialization stores each supplied value, so constructing n occupied elements takes Theta(n) work. Try a one-element or duplicate-heavy sequence before reading or changing individual positions.

slides.title: Access: read one known position
paragraphs: Reading index i returns the value stored there. Check 0 ≤ i < length before reading. Knowing a value is not the same as knowing its index: the value 4 could be absent or appear in several positions.
For contiguous storage, the address formula locates a slot directly, so valid indexed access takes O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Searching for an unknown position is a different task.

slides.title: Update: replace a value
paragraphs: An update changes the value at an existing index without changing the length or shifting other elements. Validate the index first. Updating index 1 in [3, 1, 4] to 9 gives [3, 9, 4].
One indexed write takes O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The value being written can equal another element; duplicates do not change which index is updated.

slides.title: Traversal: visit every element
paragraphs: Traversal visits the occupied positions, usually from index 0 up to length−1. A loop condition i < length avoids reading one position beyond the end. Empty input causes zero loop-body visits.
A complete traversal makes n visits, so its time is Θ(n) with O(1) auxiliary space if it only keeps a loop counter. The right panel walks through the values; no search target is required.

slides.title: Insertion: open a slot by shifting
paragraphs: To insert value x at index i, first ensure spare capacity and 0 ≤ i ≤ length. Shift elements from the end toward i so that a value is copied before its slot is overwritten. Then write x and increase length.

Inserting 9 at index 1 in [3, 1, 4] yields [3, 9, 1, 4]. Inserting at the end shifts zero elements; inserting at the beginning may shift n. Worst-case time is Θ(n), with O(1) auxiliary space in reserved storage.

slides.title: Deletion: close the gap
paragraphs: Deletion requires an existing index: 0 ≤ i < length. Preserve the removed value if it is needed, shift later elements left, and reduce length. The old last slot is no longer part of the logical sequence.
Deleting index 1 from [3, 1, 4] leaves [3, 4]. A missing index or an empty input must be handled before moving values. Worst-case time is Θ(n); deleting the last element needs no shifts.

slides.title: Capacity and important alternatives
paragraphs: A spare physical slot is not yet a readable logical element. For length 3 and capacity 5, reading index 3 is invalid, while inserting at index 3 is valid. When length equals capacity, insertion needs an explicit policy.

The in-place example rejects a full array. The alternative allocates a new sequence of length n+1 and copies values around the new element: Θ(n) time and Θ(n) extra/output storage. Growable language collections can resize internally; this does not make every individual insertion O(1).

slides.title: Boundary checks before movement
paragraphs: For reading, updating or deleting, valid indices stop at n−1. For insertion, n is also valid because it appends after the last element. A negative index is invalid in these examples, even though some languages offer negative-index syntax.

Try the empty and one-element cases. Insertion into an empty sequence at 0 works when capacity is available. Access or deletion in an empty sequence must report an error. Do not confuse zero-based index 0 with an empty collection.

faqs.question: Is index 3 the same as value 3?
faqs.answer: No. An index identifies a position. The value stored there might be 3, another value, or no valid element if the index is outside the logical length.

faqs.question: Why does insertion shift from right to left?
faqs.answer: Moving left to right would overwrite a value before it had been copied to its new slot. Starting at the right protects the remaining values.

faqs.question: Is index equal to length valid?
faqs.answer: Only for insertion at the end. Access, update and deletion need an existing element, so they require index < length.

faqs.question: Why is capacity different from length?
faqs.answer: Capacity counts reserved slots; length counts occupied elements. Unused capacity is not part of the readable sequence.

modules.title: Searching
modules.description: Compare a complete scan with sorted-range halving.

slides.title: Find a value and define “not found”
paragraphs: Searching asks whether a target occurs and, if so, where. A result must distinguish index 0 (a valid first match) from no match. Our sequence examples return −1 for no match.
Duplicates need a policy. Linear search below returns the first occurrence. The binary search example can return any matching occurrence. The target does not have to be positive or unique.

slides.title: Linear search: inspect in order
paragraphs: Inspect each element from left to right and compare it with the target. Before index i, all earlier values have been checked. Stop at the first equal value; if the scan ends, the target is absent.
This works on unsorted input. Best-case time is Θ(1); worst-case time is Θ(n), with O(1) auxiliary space. In an empty sequence the loop runs zero times and returns −1.

slides.title: Before binary search: establish ordering
paragraphs: Binary search is justified only when the input is ordered using the same comparison as the search. Here it must be ascending. Comparing a middle value can then rule out all values on one side. Without ordering, that conclusion is invalid.
Sorting first has a cost, so binary search is not automatically the best choice for one search of unsorted data. The visualization rejects unsorted input rather than silently changing it.

slides.title: Binary search: keep a possible interval
paragraphs: Maintain an inclusive interval [lo, hi]. Compare the middle slot. If it is smaller than the target, set lo = mid+1; if larger, set hi = mid−1. If equal, return mid. Each unsuccessful comparison removes the middle slot and half of the remaining range.
Stop when lo > hi. This ensures progress and handles missing targets and empty inputs. Worst-case time is Θ(log n); the iterative example uses O(1) auxiliary space.

slides.title: Variants: recursion and duplicate boundaries
paragraphs: A recursive binary search expresses the same shrinking interval as smaller calls. It still requires sorted input, but uses O(log n) call-stack space in the worst case instead of the iterative version’s O(1) extra space.
To find the first duplicate, do not stop permanently at equality: remember that candidate and continue searching the left range. An “any match” result should not be presented as “first match.”

faqs.question: Why can’t binary search just try an unsorted input?
faqs.answer: Discarding half of the input depends on ordering. A smaller middle value says nothing about the other side of an unsorted sequence.

faqs.question: Why use mid+1 and mid−1?
faqs.answer: The middle value was already checked. Excluding it guarantees that the interval shrinks after an unsuccessful comparison.

faqs.question: Does binary search always return the first duplicate?
faqs.answer: No. This version returns any equal middle slot. First-occurrence search needs a different boundary rule.

faqs.question: Is −1 a possible found index?
faqs.answer: Not with our zero-based, nonnegative index convention. It is reserved as the no-match result.

modules.title: Sorting
modules.description: Build sorted prefixes, merge runs and partition around pivots.

slides.title: Sorting and what must be preserved
paragraphs: Sorting rearranges values into a chosen order. Ascending order means every value is no greater than the next. Correctness also requires preserving the input’s values and multiplicities: [2, 2, 1] must become [1, 2, 2], not [1, 2].
A stable sort preserves the original order of items with equal keys. With plain identical numbers this is invisible; imagine each number carries a name to see why stability can matter.

slides.title: Insertion sort: grow a sorted prefix
paragraphs: Keep positions before i sorted. Remember the next key, shift only strictly larger prefix values right, and put the key into the resulting gap. Equal keys are not shifted past one another, so this version is stable.
An already sorted input needs a linear number of comparisons. Reverse order can need about n(n−1)/2 shifts: Θ(n²) time. Auxiliary space is O(1).

slides.title: Merge sort: combine sorted runs
paragraphs: Merging takes two sorted runs and repeatedly chooses the smaller front value. Choosing the left run on ties preserves stability. Bottom-up merge sort begins with length-one runs and doubles the run width after each pass.

Each pass processes n elements and there are about log₂ n passes: Θ(n log n) time. A temporary buffer takes Θ(n) auxiliary space. Read events may fill the buffer before writes update the displayed sequence.

slides.title: Quicksort: partition, then sort parts
paragraphs: This partition uses the final element as pivot. During the scan, values before the boundary are ≤ pivot; checked values after it are > pivot. Swapping the pivot into its final slot separates two smaller sorting tasks.

Quicksort is not stable here. Balanced partitions give Θ(n log n) time, but sorted or all-equal input with a final-element pivot can give Θ(n²). Recursive examples can use Θ(n) stack space in the worst case; the visualization uses an explicit bounded range stack.

slides.title: Choose variants by their guarantees
paragraphs: Top-down merge sort recursively splits the input before merging; bottom-up merge sort doubles run widths. Both use a merging buffer and Θ(n log n) time. The alternative merge example includes the complete recursive setup.

For quicksort, pivot selection and three-way partitioning can reduce particular bad cases, but changing a pivot policy alone does not make stability automatic. Insertion sort can be useful for small or nearly sorted inputs. Avoid declaring a universal “fastest” sort without a workload and measurement.

slides.title: Compare with identical input
paragraphs: Run the same input through insertion, merge and quicksort. Compare the number and kinds of operations, not animation duration. A swap, a buffer read and a write represent different work, so report their counts separately.

Try sorted, reverse-sorted and duplicate-heavy inputs. These expose adaptivity, pivot imbalance and stable tie handling. Empty and one-element inputs are already sorted and still need a correct completion result.

slides.title: Another in-place choice: heap sort
paragraphs: Heap sort builds a max-heap and moves its largest value to a sorted suffix. The Heaps and Priority Queues module teaches the representation, construction and sift-down proof in full. Explore its pages before using this alternative. The visualization here calls exactly the same heap-sort implementation.

faqs.question: Does sorted output alone prove correctness?
faqs.answer: No. The output must also contain exactly the original values with the same multiplicities.

faqs.question: Why does insertion sort shift only larger values?
faqs.answer: Shifting equal values past the remembered key would reverse some equal-key order. A strict greater-than comparison preserves stability.

faqs.question: Why can quicksort be quadratic?
faqs.answer: A poor pivot can repeatedly leave a subproblem of size n−1. Adding those scans gives a quadratic total.

faqs.question: Is a faster animation a faster algorithm?
faqs.answer: No. Playback pace is a presentation setting. Use well-defined operation counts or a controlled execution benchmark.

modules.title: Singly linked lists
modules.description: Follow and change links without shifting a row of values.

slides.title: A sequence joined by links
paragraphs: A singly linked list consists of nodes. Each node stores a value and a next link to another node, or null at the end. The head identifies the first node; an empty list has a null head.
Links describe relationships, not neighboring array slots. The nodes need not be physically contiguous. Unlike an array, finding the node at index i normally requires following i links.

slides.title: Keep a route to every node
paragraphs: Traversal begins at the head and repeatedly follows next until null. To change the link entering a node, remember its predecessor. A singly linked node does not automatically know which node comes before it.

The diagrams show conceptual links, not browser addresses. Preserve reachability: overwriting the only link to a node can lose the remaining chain. Unlinking and freeing a removed node are separate responsibilities in languages with manual memory management.

slides.title: Insert without losing the successor
paragraphs: Locate the predecessor of the insertion position. First point the new node to the old successor; then point the predecessor to the new node. At index 0, replace the head instead.

Finding the predecessor can take Θ(n) time; relinking after it is known takes O(1). Inserting at index 0 also works for an empty list. These examples use zero-based positions and allow insertion at length.

slides.title: Delete: repair the chain and head
paragraphs: To delete an existing position, make its predecessor point to the removed node’s successor. Deleting the head updates the head itself. Removing the only node leaves an empty list.

Do not discard the removed node’s next link before repairing the chain. The C and C++ examples release removed nodes; the full snippet includes its node type. The indexed operation is O(n) to locate the node.

slides.title: Search follows links
paragraphs: Compare each node value and follow next until a match or null. Duplicates are allowed and the first matching node is returned. A null result means no match; it is not a node containing value zero.
Worst-case time is Θ(n), with O(1) auxiliary space. Knowing a value does not reveal a node’s position or predecessor.

slides.title: Traverse the whole chain
paragraphs: Visit a node before moving to its successor. The empty list produces zero visits. Following links costs Θ(n) for n nodes and needs only one current-node reference.
Unlike indexed arrays, repeatedly starting at the head to fetch each position can make an apparently simple loop quadratic. Keep the current link while traversing.

slides.title: Sentinels and tail references
paragraphs: A sentinel is an extra dummy node before the first data node. It can make head insertion/deletion use the same predecessor rule as other positions, but it is not a data element and changes the representation.
A tail reference can make append O(1) when maintained correctly. It must be updated when the last node is removed. Our default examples use an explicit head and do not assume a tail or sentinel.

faqs.question: Why can changing next lose nodes?
faqs.answer: If next is the only route to the remaining chain and you overwrite it before saving the successor, that route is lost.

faqs.question: When must the head change?
faqs.answer: Insertion at index 0 and deletion of the first node change the head. Removing the only node sets it to null.

faqs.question: Is deleting a known value always constant time?
faqs.answer: No. This singly linked list must find both the target and its predecessor unless the needed references are already available.

faqs.question: What should an empty list do?
faqs.answer: Traversal and search stop immediately; head insertion at index 0 is allowed; deleting a nonexistent position is an error.

modules.title: Stacks
modules.description: Learn last-in-first-out order and safe boundary operations.

slides.title: The last item in is the first out
paragraphs: A stack stores a sequence with access at one end, called the top. Push adds at the top; pop removes the top; peek reads it without removal. A pile of plates is a useful model.
If you push 2, then 4, then 6, the first pop returns 6. A stack describes allowed behavior; it can be implemented with an array or linked nodes.

slides.title: Length identifies the top
paragraphs: In a bounded array-backed stack, occupied values lie at indices 0 through length−1. The top is at length−1 when the stack is nonempty. Capacity limits how many values can be stored.
Empty and full are different conditions. Empty means there is no item to read/remove; full means a bounded implementation has no room for another push.

slides.title: Push: check capacity, then append
paragraphs: Push checks for space, stores the new value at index length, then increases length. It does not reorder earlier elements. If capacity is exhausted, report the failure without overwriting a live value.
The bounded array example takes O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space for one valid push. The visualization holds at most 32 values.

slides.title: Pop: remove and return the top
paragraphs: Check that length is positive before reducing it. The removed value is the old last element. Popping [2, 4, 6] returns 6 and leaves [2, 4].
Popping an empty stack is underflow. An error or explicit empty result is safer than treating an arbitrary zero as a removed value. A valid pop is O(1).

slides.title: Peek leaves the stack unchanged
paragraphs: Peek reads the top value and preserves length and order. It needs the same nonempty check as pop. Repeated peeks return the same value unless another operation changes the stack.
The operation is O(1). A linked implementation can also push/pop at the head in O(1), but each node requires its own storage and allocation handling.

faqs.question: Does peek remove a value?
faqs.answer: No. Peek reads the top while pop removes it. Both reject an empty stack.

faqs.question: Is zero an underflow marker?
faqs.answer: Not by itself: zero can be a legitimate stored value. Use a separate status, exception or optional result.

faqs.question: Why do call stacks relate to this structure?
faqs.answer: The most recent unfinished function call returns first. Each recursive call adds another active frame before earlier calls can finish.

modules.title: Queues
modules.description: Track first-in-first-out order and compare representations.

slides.title: The first item in is the first out
paragraphs: A queue adds at the back and removes from the front. People waiting in a single orderly line illustrate first-in-first-out (FIFO) behavior. Enqueue adds; dequeue removes; inspect reads the front without removing it.
Enqueueing 2, 4 and 6 in that order means the first dequeue returns 2, regardless of which value is largest.

slides.title: Locate the front and the back
paragraphs: Our compact array representation stores the front at index 0 and the back at length−1. Enqueue appends. Dequeue shifts remaining values left to keep the front at index 0.
FIFO is the behavior, not a promise that every representation has the same cost. Empty means length is zero; full means length equals the bounded capacity.

slides.title: Enqueue at the back
paragraphs: Check for capacity, write the value after the current back, then increase length. Earlier arrivals keep their order. One enqueue in reserved storage takes O(1) time.
A full queue must reject the operation or grow through a documented policy. Silently overwriting the front would lose an arrival.

slides.title: Dequeue the oldest value
paragraphs: Preserve the front value, shift each later value one slot left, and decrease length. Dequeueing [2, 4, 6] returns 2 and leaves [4, 6]. Check for underflow before reading.
This compact representation takes O(n) time for dequeue and O(1) auxiliary space. The single conceptual dequeue in the visualization includes these shifts; it is not a constant-time CPU instruction.

slides.title: Inspect without removal
paragraphs: Inspect returns the front but changes neither length nor order. The empty check matters even if a previously used physical slot still contains an old value: only logical elements belong to the queue.
In this representation inspection takes O(1) time and auxiliary space.

slides.title: Alternative: a circular buffer
paragraphs: A circular queue keeps a head index and a size. The next back slot is (head + size) modulo capacity. Modulo means the remainder: after the final slot, the index wraps around to zero.

Dequeue advances head instead of shifting values, so both enqueue and dequeue can be O(1). Keep size to distinguish full from empty when indices wrap. The alternative example implements these rules; the compact shifting visualization remains the same FIFO abstraction.

faqs.question: Why does the compact dequeue take O(n)?
faqs.answer: It shifts the remaining values. FIFO behavior does not require shifting; a circular representation avoids it.

faqs.question: Do enqueue and dequeue use the same end?
faqs.answer: No. Enqueue uses the back and dequeue uses the front. A stack instead adds and removes at its top.

faqs.question: Why retain a size in a circular buffer?
faqs.answer: Wrapped indices alone can look the same for empty and full states. Size explicitly distinguishes them and enforces capacity.

modules.title: Binary search trees
modules.description: Use ordering to navigate, update and traverse a tree.

slides.title: Branch using comparisons
paragraphs: A binary tree node has at most a left child and a right child. A binary search tree (BST) adds an ordering rule: every value in the left subtree is smaller, and every value in the right subtree is larger.
The root is the first node to inspect. An empty tree has no root. This module ignores duplicate insertions, making the ordering strict.

slides.title: Subtrees and height
paragraphs: A subtree contains a node and all nodes below it. The ordering rule applies to all descendants, not only immediate children. Height h describes the longest root-to-leaf route.
Search, insertion and deletion follow routes of length O(h). An unbalanced tree can become a chain with h proportional to n; logarithmic behavior is not guaranteed. Traversals visit all n nodes.

slides.title: Insert at a missing child
paragraphs: Start at the root and compare. Go left for a smaller value, right for a larger one, and stop without adding a node on equality. Attach a new node where the required child is missing.
Inserting into an empty tree creates the root. The ordering invariant must hold for every ancestor, not just the parent.

slides.title: Search follows the ordering rule
paragraphs: Compare with the current node. An equal value is a match; otherwise descend into the only subtree that could contain the target. Reaching a missing child means no match.
A search costs O(h). Duplicate handling is an explicit policy; a different BST could count duplicate values, but this lesson does not add duplicate nodes.

slides.title: Delete a leaf
paragraphs: First search for the target. A leaf has no children, so its parent’s corresponding child becomes null. If the target is the only root, the whole tree becomes empty.
A missing target leaves the tree unchanged. Deletion must update the link that enters the target; deleting a local reference alone does not repair the tree.

slides.title: Delete a node with one child
paragraphs: Replace the link entering the target with a link to its only child. This preserves every descendant without needing to copy an entire subtree. If the target is the root, its child becomes the new root.
Check left and right cases symmetrically. The full deletion function handles leaf, one-child and two-child cases together.

slides.title: Delete a node with two children
paragraphs: The inorder successor is the smallest value in the right subtree: follow left links from the right child. It has no left child. Replacing the target by this successor preserves ordering, but the successor must be removed from its old position.

The example copies the successor value and recursively removes that value; the diagram relinks the successor node. Both preserve the BST value ordering, but node identities can differ. Do not confuse a node’s identity with its stored value.

slides.title: Inorder traversal: left, node, right
paragraphs: Visit the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. The BST ordering rule makes this output ascending, regardless of the shape of the tree.
Each node is visited once, so traversal takes Θ(n) time. Recursive examples use O(h) call-stack space. An empty tree produces no visits.

slides.title: Preorder traversal: node, left, right
paragraphs: Visit the node before its children. Preorder exposes the root before exploring its subtrees and can describe the shape when paired with enough structural information.
Preorder is not sorted order. It still visits each node once and uses O(h) recursive stack space.

slides.title: Postorder traversal: left, right, node
paragraphs: Visit both subtrees before the node. This order is useful when a parent’s work depends on its children, such as releasing a manually allocated tree.
Postorder is not the reverse of inorder in general. All three traversal orders require Θ(n) time for n nodes.

slides.title: Shape changes the cost
paragraphs: Inserting sorted distinct values can create a chain. A balanced-tree policy can keep height logarithmic, but rotations and balancing rules are future topics, not operations implemented in this module.
The iterative search example uses O(1) auxiliary space. Recursive insert/delete examples can use O(h) call-stack space. State both tree shape and implementation when explaining cost.

faqs.question: What happens to duplicates?
faqs.answer: Insertion is ignored on equality in this module. Counting duplicates or choosing a tie direction would be different documented policies.

faqs.question: Why not replace a deleted two-child node by any child?
faqs.answer: That can lose a subtree or violate ordering. The inorder successor gives a replacement value with a specific ordering guarantee.

faqs.question: Is a BST always logarithmic?
faqs.answer: No. Cost depends on height; an unbalanced tree can be a chain of n nodes.

faqs.question: Why is inorder sorted but preorder is not?
faqs.answer: Inorder visits all smaller descendants before the node and all larger descendants after it. Preorder deliberately visits the node first.

modules.title: Graphs and paths
modules.description: Model connections, explore reachable places and find weighted distances.

slides.title: Vertices and edges model connections
paragraphs: A graph consists of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections). A road map, friendship network or prerequisite diagram can be modeled this way. Labels identify vertices; their numeric order is not a traversal rule.
A directed edge can be followed only from its source to its target. An undirected edge works both ways. A weight is a cost attached to an edge; zero is a valid weight.

slides.title: Represent adjacency explicitly
paragraphs: An adjacency matrix has a row and column for each vertex and records which edges exist. Presence is separate from weight, so weight zero does not mean “missing.” With V vertices, matrix storage is O(V²).

An adjacency list stores outgoing neighbors instead and can use O(V+E) storage for E edges. The default examples here use a matrix to match the diagrams’ neighbor scans; the BFS alternative demonstrates a list after these representation ideas.

slides.title: Build and edit a graph
paragraphs: Add/remove vertices and set/remove edges with the controls. Labels are unique integers from 1 to 31, with at most 16 vertices. Removing a vertex also removes its incident edges. Setting an existing edge replaces its weight instead of adding a parallel edge.
Self-loops are allowed. In undirected mode an edge is symmetric. Changing direction mode rebuilds the selected graph interpretation, so inspect its arrows before choosing a start vertex.

slides.title: Track visits and disconnected components
paragraphs: A cycle can lead back to an earlier vertex. Track visited vertices to avoid repeated work or an infinite traversal. A disconnected graph may contain vertices unreachable from a chosen source; one source-based traversal does not claim to visit them all.
Neighbor order affects the visit order when several choices are possible. Our diagrams follow input order. Direction matters: an incoming edge is not necessarily an outgoing route.

slides.title: BFS: explore in layers
paragraphs: Breadth-first search uses a FIFO queue. Mark a vertex when enqueuing it so it enters the queue once. Dequeue it, visit it, then enqueue unvisited outgoing neighbors. This explores one edge-distance layer before the next.

BFS ignores weights. With a matrix, scanning all potential neighbors gives O(V²) time; an adjacency-list version gives O(V+E) for a complete reachable traversal. Auxiliary visited/queue storage is O(V).

slides.title: DFS: follow a branch and backtrack
paragraphs: Depth-first search follows an unvisited outgoing neighbor before returning to earlier choices. An explicit stack remembers the active path and which neighbor to try next. When a vertex has no unvisited outgoing neighbor, backtrack.
DFS also ignores weights and only visits reachable vertices. Matrix neighbor scans take O(V²) time; the active stack and visited information need O(V) auxiliary space.

slides.title: Dijkstra: settle shortest distances
paragraphs: For nonnegative edge weights, repeatedly select the unsettled vertex with smallest tentative distance. Its distance is final. Relax an outgoing edge by replacing a neighbor’s distance when current distance + weight is smaller.

The source distance is zero; unreachable vertices retain infinity. This implementation uses linear minimum selection and a matrix, taking O(V²) time and O(V) auxiliary distance/visited storage. All negative edges are rejected, including unreachable negative edges.

slides.title: Choose the right question and prerequisites
paragraphs: BFS answers reachability and unweighted edge-distance questions; DFS explores branches and backtracking; Dijkstra minimizes total nonnegative edge weight. A path with fewer edges need not have a smaller total weight.

Negative weights can invalidate the settled-distance argument. They require a different shortest-path method, which is outside this module. Do not “fix” them by silently taking absolute values. Try disconnected vertices, zero weights and directed one-way edges.

faqs.question: Why mark BFS vertices on enqueue?
faqs.answer: Two different neighbors could otherwise enqueue the same vertex before it is processed. Marking immediately prevents duplicate queue entries.

faqs.question: Did the algorithm fail if a vertex was not visited?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. It may be disconnected or unreachable along outgoing directed edges from the chosen source.

faqs.question: Can Dijkstra use negative weights if there is no negative cycle?
faqs.answer: No. The nonnegative-edge guarantee is needed for its settled-distance rule; absence of negative cycles alone is not enough.

faqs.question: Does weight zero mean no edge?
faqs.answer: No. Presence is stored separately. A zero-cost edge is valid and Dijkstra can follow it.

faqs.question: Does BFS find cheapest weighted paths?
faqs.answer: No. BFS minimizes edge count in an unweighted interpretation. Weighted costs require a suitable shortest-path algorithm.

modules.title: Hash Tables
modules.description: Map keys to values, resolve collisions and rebuild buckets.

slides.title: Find a value by its key
paragraphs: A key identifies a record; its value is the information attached to that key. A student number might identify a score. A hash table maps keys to values instead of treating a key as an array index. The keys 10 and 100000 need not require 100001 array slots.

You will compute buckets, resolve collisions with two representations, insert/update/delete entries, and explain how table size changes the cost. Arrays and Foundations supply the ideas of indices, capacity and operation counts.
bullets: Compute normalized bucket indices
Trace chaining and probing
Explain deletion and rehashing

slides.title: Turn an integer key into a bucket
paragraphs: A hash function deterministically maps a key to a bucket index. Here bucket(k) = ((k % capacity) + capacity) % capacity. The second remainder normalizes negative remainders in C, C++, Java and JavaScript; Python already gives a nonnegative remainder for positive capacity.

With eight buckets, -1 and 7 both map to 7. Equal buckets are a collision, not proof that the keys are equal. Always compare keys. Input is alternating key,value integers, for example -1,90,7,80. Values and keys are bounded at ±100000.

slides.title: Separate chaining keeps colliding entries
paragraphs: Each bucket names the first entry in a linked chain. An entry stores key, value and next. Search follows the links and compares keys until it finds equality or reaches the end. Entries have stable conceptual IDs; their links are not browser addresses.

Inserting a new key at the head costs constant link work after the bucket is chosen. Finding whether it already exists may traverse the whole chain. Try keys 0,8,16 with eight buckets and count the comparisons.

slides.title: Insertion of a duplicate updates its value
paragraphs: This map has one entry per key. Inserting key 8 with value 99 replaces the value for 8 without increasing the number of entries. It does not add a second copy. A value of zero is valid, so success must be reported separately from the returned value.
The editable Key field selects the key; New value is the value written by this operation. Missing lookups return a separate not-found result and leave the table unchanged.

slides.title: Delete without losing the remaining chain
paragraphs: To delete a chained entry, make its predecessor point to its successor. Deleting the first entry changes the bucket head. The other links stay reachable. Empty buckets and missing keys need no unlinking.
For 0→8→16 in one bucket, removing 8 must still leave a path from 0 to 16. Our insertion-at-head representation may display this order in reverse, but the same reachability rule applies.

slides.title: Delete and follow the remaining links
paragraphs: This compound worked example removes key 8, then searches for 16 in the surviving chain. Compare it with the probing tombstone experiment. Chaining repairs an actual conceptual link instead of leaving a tombstone; both strategies keep unrelated keys reachable.

slides.title: Linear probing searches neighboring slots
paragraphs: Linear probing stores entries directly in a slot array. Try the home bucket first, then (home+1) % capacity, then the next slot, wrapping around. An occupied slot with a different key means continue. An empty never-used slot means the key is absent.

A probe is bounded by capacity, even when no empty slot is encountered. Closely spaced collisions form clusters and can make later operations slower. Compare this layout with separate chaining on the same keys.

slides.title: Build an open-addressed table
paragraphs: Each missing key starts at its normalized home slot and advances across occupied slots. Try colliding keys -1,7,15 and compare the resulting slot layout with chaining. Construction itself uses the same bounded insertion rule as later updates.

slides.title: Delete an occupied probing slot
paragraphs: Deleting key 8 leaves a tombstone, reduces live size, and preserves the probe path for other keys. A missing deletion does not change the table. The tombstone page’s delete-then-lookup experiment lets you inspect the continued search in the same run.

slides.title: A deletion marker preserves the search path
paragraphs: Suppose keys 0,8,16 occupy slots 0,1,2. If slot 1 is cleared to never-used empty after deleting 8, a lookup for 16 stops too early at slot 1. A tombstone says an entry was deleted here: keep searching.
This experiment deletes Key, then looks up the second key supplied in Lookup key after deletion. Delete 8 and find 16. The tombstone is neither an occupied entry nor a stopping empty slot.

slides.title: Probe insertion and updates
paragraphs: Search for an existing key before inserting: an equal key is updated in place. Otherwise remember the first tombstone, keep checking for duplicates, and insert into that tombstone or the first empty slot.

Stopping immediately at a tombstone can create duplicate keys later in the same probe sequence. This bounded demonstration grows conservatively before inserting a missing key if its load would exceed 0.75.

slides.title: Grow the capacity and recompute every bucket
paragraphs: Load factor is number of live entries divided by capacity. Six entries in eight slots have load 0.75. Our policy doubles capacity before an insertion would exceed 0.75. Manual Rehash also doubles capacity. The teaching table starts at eight buckets and grows at most to 64.

Changing capacity changes the remainder calculation. Move each live entry into its new bucket; copying an old slot index is incorrect. Rehashing removes tombstones and preserves keys, values and entry IDs. Watch old placements while new buckets fill.

slides.title: Rehash a linked-bucket representation
paragraphs: Chaining also recomputes the bucket of every live key when capacity changes. Entry IDs and values remain stable, but next links are rebuilt for the new bucket heads. Rehashing is not specific to probing; its purpose is to change the bucket layout and control load.

slides.title: Expected cost needs assumptions
paragraphs: With well-distributed hashes and a controlled load factor, lookup/insertion/deletion have expected O(1) cost. A fixed remainder hash can distribute adversarial multiples of capacity badly: all entries may collide, giving O(n) worst-case work. Expected is an assumption about inputs or hashing, not a promise for every key.

One rehash takes O(n + capacity) work to initialize buckets and move entries; doubling spreads occasional rebuild cost across many insertions. Our tiny fixed maximum is an input safety limit, not an asymptotic complexity claim. Tombstones lengthen probes even when the live load is low.

slides.title: Reinsert after unlinking
paragraphs: This compound run deletes key 8, then inserts key 8 with the new value. The entry count first falls and then recovers. A probing insertion remembers a tombstone but continues checking the rest of the sequence for an existing equal key before reusing that slot. Chaining creates a new entry linked at the bucket head. A deleted entry ID is retired; the new entry receives a new conceptual identity.

slides.title: Reuse a tombstone after searching for duplicates
paragraphs: This compound run deletes key 8, then inserts key 8 with the new value. The entry count first falls and then recovers. A probing insertion remembers a tombstone but continues checking the rest of the sequence for an existing equal key before reusing that slot. Chaining creates a new entry linked at the bucket head. A deleted entry ID is retired; the new entry receives a new conceptual identity.

faqs.question: Does a collision overwrite another key?
faqs.answer: No. Only equality of the actual key means update. Chaining and probing keep distinct colliding keys.

faqs.question: Can I erase a probed slot to empty?
faqs.answer: Use a tombstone or repair the whole probe cluster. A never-used empty slot would make later lookups stop early.

faqs.question: Why did my bucket change after resizing?
faqs.answer: The capacity participates in the hash calculation. Recompute each live key’s bucket.

faqs.question: Is O(1) guaranteed?
faqs.answer: No. It is expected under distribution and load assumptions; collision-heavy inputs can require a linear scan.

modules.title: Heaps and Priority Queues
modules.description: Maintain priorities with complete trees and linked array views.

slides.title: A complete tree of priorities
paragraphs: A priority queue removes the most urgent item instead of the oldest item. A min-heap treats the smallest number as most urgent; a max-heap treats the largest as most urgent. A complete binary tree fills levels from left to right with no gaps.

You will connect an array to that tree, repair ordering with sifts, compare construction methods, and use the same operations for heap sort. Duplicate priorities are allowed. This numeric heap promises no stable ordering among equal-priority records.
bullets: Relate heap arrays and trees
Maintain min/max ordering
Build, insert, extract and sort

slides.title: Array indices describe tree links
paragraphs: With zero-based indices, children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2. The parent of a non-root i is floor((i-1)/2). A child index outside the active heap extent means that child is absent. No explicit link objects are required.

Heap order constrains each parent and its children. It does not order siblings or different branches: [1,4,2] is a valid min-heap but is not sorted. The array and tree highlight the same compared or swapped indices.

slides.title: Min-heaps and max-heaps reverse priority
paragraphs: Min-heaps require parent ≤ child. Max-heaps require parent ≥ child. The shape is unchanged; the comparison changes. Equal values need no swap. When children tie, the demonstration chooses the left child, but equal-priority extraction has no record-order guarantee.

Every run first builds the supplied values into the requested heap, then performs the selected operation. Displayed counters include this preparation. The per-operation bounds assume a heap has already been built.

slides.title: Bottom-up construction is linear
paragraphs: Leaves already satisfy heap order. Start at floor(n/2)-1, the last parent, and sift each parent down toward the root. Many nodes are near the bottom and can move only one or two levels.

Summing the work by height gives n/4 one-level moves, n/8 two-level moves, and progressively fewer longer paths. This sum is O(n), not n times log n. Inserting n elements one at a time instead costs O(n log n) in the worst case.

slides.title: Insert at the end, then sift up
paragraphs: Append the new value at the first free array slot to preserve completeness. Compare it to its parent. If the child has higher priority, swap and repeat toward the root. Stop at correct order or the root.
For a built heap, at most the tree height is crossed: O(log n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space for iterative repair. This lab holds at most 32 values and rejects insertion when full.

slides.title: The same sift with maximum priority
paragraphs: Insert 12 into a max-heap and follow it upward while it exceeds its parent. Smaller values stay below larger parents. The complete-tree shape still follows array length.
Compare this run with min insertion on identical values. Swapping only on a strict priority improvement avoids unnecessary movement for equal values.

slides.title: Peek reads without removing
paragraphs: Peek returns the root in O(1) time after construction. It changes neither the heap length nor its ordering. Empty heaps have no root: the operation reports an error rather than inventing a sentinel value that might also be valid data.

slides.title: Inspect maximum priority
paragraphs: A max-heap peek returns a largest value without removing it, just as min peek returns a smallest value. It is O(1) after construction and rejects an empty heap. The complete-tree shape and physical array length stay unchanged.

slides.title: Extract the root and sift down
paragraphs: Save the root result, move the last value into the root slot, and shorten the active prefix. Compare the two children, choose the higher-priority child, then compare with the parent. Swap only when needed and continue downward.

Choosing an arbitrary child can leave the other child out of order. Extraction from an existing heap is O(log n) worst-case time, with O(1) iterative extra space. A singleton heap becomes empty after extraction.

slides.title: Extract the maximum
paragraphs: The same repair chooses the larger child for a max-heap. The removed value is shown separately from the remaining array. Repeated max extractions produce nonincreasing priorities; min extractions produce nondecreasing priorities.

slides.title: Use a max-heap to sort in place
paragraphs: Build a max-heap, swap its root with the last active element, shrink the heap extent, and sift down again. The suffix outside the tree is sorted and no longer participates in repair. Repeat until the entire array is ascending.

Heap sort takes O(n log n) worst-case time and O(1) auxiliary space with iterative sifts. It is not stable: equal values can change relative record order. This is the same implementation linked from Sorting.

slides.title: Priority queues in applications
paragraphs: Schedulers, event simulation and shortest-path algorithms often need the next smallest priority. A heap provides efficient insertion and extraction, but searching an arbitrary key remains O(n) unless another index is maintained.

A priority queue can select Dijkstra’s next tentative distance efficiently. The existing graph lesson actually uses a scan of all unsettled vertices and an adjacency matrix, giving O(V²) work. It does not secretly switch to a heap. A heap-based adjacency-list variant requires tracking updated or stale queue entries; it is a future graph extension.

faqs.question: Why is my heap array not sorted?
faqs.answer: Only parent-child priority is guaranteed. Siblings and distant branches can appear in either order.

faqs.question: Is building a heap always O(n log n)?
faqs.answer: Repeated insertion has that worst-case bound. Bottom-up construction is O(n) because most nodes are close to leaves.

faqs.question: Which duplicate comes out first?
faqs.answer: This numeric heap has no stable tie ordering. Use a secondary sequence number if a real application needs FIFO ties.

faqs.question: Do operation counters exclude setup?
faqs.answer: No. A run first constructs the heap; the displayed comparisons include construction. Per-operation bounds assume an existing heap.

faqs.question: Does the graph lesson already use this queue?
faqs.answer: No. Its Dijkstra implementation scans unsettled vertices in a matrix representation.

modules.title: Recursion
modules.description: Trace call frames, base cases, returns and repeated subproblems.

slides.title: Solve a smaller instance of the same problem
paragraphs: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller instance. A base case answers a small instance directly. A recursive case must make measurable progress toward a base case. Merely writing a base case does not guarantee that future calls ever reach it.

This module uses stack frames and sorted binary search from its explicit prerequisites. You will trace factorial, array sum, recursive binary search and branching Fibonacci, including return values and maximum simultaneous depth.
bullets: State a terminating recursive contract
Trace locals and return values
Separate total work from maximum stack depth

slides.title: Factorial multiplies while unwinding
paragraphs: For nonnegative n, factorial(0)=1 and factorial(n)=n×factorial(n-1). For 4, calls descend through 4,3,2,1; returns unwind as 1,2,6,24. The current frame waits until the smaller call returns.

This lab accepts n from 0 to 12. Then 12! = 479001600 fits signed 32-bit arithmetic; 13! does not. Negative n is rejected before execution. The displayed functions enforce this contract; wider accumulators do not make arbitrary n safe.

slides.title: Each call keeps its own unfinished work
paragraphs: A frame stores arguments, local values and where execution resumes after a child returns. Two frames may use the same variable names but hold different values. The active frame is on top of the conceptual stack, shown at the bottom of the list.

A waiting frame records where it resumes after a child returns. Call IDs and parent IDs show nesting, not actual addresses. A return removes one active frame and passes a value to its caller. The call-tree record remains visible for review; branching calls keep the first answer while evaluating their second child.

slides.title: Recursively sum a prefix
paragraphs: Define sum(a,n) as the sum of the first n values. The empty prefix returns 0. For n>0, sum(a,n)=sum(a,n-1)+a[n-1]. The original array is unchanged. For [2,-1,4], returns are 0,2,1,5.

This visits n elements in O(n) time and keeps O(n) active call-stack space. An iterative scan can use O(1) extra space instead. Here n≤32 and |value|≤100000, so the magnitude of a sum is at most 3200000.

slides.title: Recursive binary search returns a location
paragraphs: The contract searches a sorted ascending array within inclusive bounds [lo,hi]. If lo>hi, return -1. Otherwise inspect mid=lo+(hi-lo)/2. Equality returns mid; a strict comparison chooses [mid+1,hi] or [lo,mid-1].

Both bounds exclude the inspected midpoint on a failed comparison, so the interval shrinks. Empty input returns -1; duplicates may return any matching index. O(log n) time and O(log n) call-stack space differ from the O(1) extra space of iterative binary search.

slides.title: Fibonacci has two recursive children
paragraphs: Define F(0)=0, F(1)=1, and F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2) for n≥2. The first child returns before the second begins; the parent keeps the first return in a saved local. For F(4), the two child answers are 2 and 1, yielding 3.

The tree repeats smaller calls, such as F(2). The number of calls grows exponentially, bounded above by O(2^n), while maximum simultaneous depth is O(n). Total calls and active depth are different measurements. This lab limits n to 0..10 (at most 177 calls), far before numeric overflow or excessive animation.

slides.title: Choose a decreasing measure
paragraphs: For factorial and Fibonacci, n decreases toward 0 or 1. For array sum, the prefix length decreases. For binary search, the candidate interval becomes strictly shorter. A function that calls itself with the same argument never makes this progress.

Invalid inputs are rejected before starting. Do not attempt an infinite call chain: these worked examples use small input limits so you can follow every call and return. Reset starts again with the original input and an empty call stack.

slides.title: Count work and peak storage separately
paragraphs: Factorial and prefix sum form one chain: linear work and linear stack depth. Binary search follows only one of its two possible halves, so work and depth are logarithmic. Naive Fibonacci follows both branches, causing repeated work even though only one path is active at a time.

Remembering an already-computed Fibonacci result is called memoization. That idea motivates a later lesson; no dynamic-programming knowledge is required or assessed here. Python integers can grow, but Java/C/C++ fixed-width integers and JavaScript exact-number limits still matter. The stated lab limits make the examples agree.

faqs.question: Does every recursive function need a base case?
faqs.answer: It needs a directly answerable stopping case and progress toward it. Missing either can prevent termination.

faqs.question: Do both Fibonacci branches occupy the stack at once?
faqs.answer: The first finishes before the second runs. The parent saves its first answer, so total calls greatly exceed peak active depth.

faqs.question: Why is recursive binary search not O(1) extra space?
faqs.answer: Each unfinished call retains a frame. The halved interval creates O(log n) simultaneous frames.

faqs.question: Can I compute arbitrary factorials by choosing Python?
faqs.answer: Only the educational example language changes. The visualization uses the same documented 0..12 input contract.

modules.title: Two Pointers
modules.description: Maintain boundaries and invariants while scanning an array.

slides.title: Two positions coordinate one scan
paragraphs: A pointer here is an array index, not a raw memory address. Opposite-direction pointers start near the two ends and move inward. Same-direction pointers can separate a read position from an output position.
The key question is why a move is safe: an invariant describes what is already known before and after each iteration. You will find a sorted pair, reverse an array, and compact duplicate values.
bullets: Justify each pointer movement
Validate sorted-input assumptions
Distinguish physical storage and logical output

slides.title: Find a target pair in sorted input
paragraphs: Start left=0 and right=n-1, requiring left<right so one element is not used twice. If a[left]+a[right] is too small, every partner at or left of right is also too small for a[left], so discard left. If too large, every partner at or right of left is too large for a[right], so discard right.

For [1,2,4,7] and target 9, 1+7 is too small; moving left finds 2+7. The remaining interval contains every not-yet-excluded solution. Return one pair of indices, or no solution. Sorting is required and validated; input is never silently rearranged.

slides.title: Empty, duplicate and extreme values
paragraphs: Empty and singleton inputs cannot supply two distinct indices. Equal values can form a pair if they occupy different positions, such as [3,3] for target 6. When pointers meet without equality, no pair exists.

Use a sufficiently wide accumulator for the addition before comparing with the target. C/C++ cast before adding, and Java uses long. Our input bound means sums lie in [-200000,200000], exactly representable in JavaScript. Sorting beforehand would add O(n log n) cost and could change original indices; it is an explicit separate preparation, not part of this O(n) scan.

slides.title: Reverse in place from opposite ends
paragraphs: Swap a[left] with a[right], then increment left and decrement right. Everything strictly outside the two pointers is already in its final reversed position. Stop when the pointers meet or cross.
This operation does not require sorting. Empty and singleton inputs are already reversed. At most floor(n/2) swaps give O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, while preserving all values and duplicates.

slides.title: Read ahead while writing a unique prefix
paragraphs: In sorted input, equal values are adjacent. Keep write=1 after the first value and scan read from index 1. If a[read] differs from a[write-1], copy it to a[write] and increment write. Otherwise skip it.

Invariant: a[0..write) contains exactly one copy of each distinct value seen so far, in order, and write≤read+1. For [1,1,2,2,4], the result prefix is [1,2,4] and logical length is 3. Slots after that prefix still exist and may contain stale values; they are not part of the answer.

slides.title: Two monotone scans stay linear
paragraphs: Each pointer moves in one direction and never restarts from the beginning. Pair search and compaction therefore take O(n) time; reversal uses a linear number of swaps. None needs extra storage proportional to n.

Not every problem becomes linear merely by using two indices. The proof depends on a movement rule that safely discards work. Unsorted pair sum and unsorted adjacent compaction do not satisfy these sorted-order arguments. All equal, missing-pair, empty and boundary inputs are useful checks.

faqs.question: Are these C pointer addresses?
faqs.answer: No. The labels are conceptual positions in the array, shared by all five example languages.

faqs.question: Why can’t pair sum just use the same moves on unsorted input?
faqs.answer: The elimination proof depends on all later values being at least as large. Without order, a discarded partner could form a solution.

faqs.question: Did duplicate removal shrink the allocation?
faqs.answer: No. It reports a valid prefix length. Ignore the physical suffix; it has not been promised empty or cleared.

faqs.question: Can one position supply both numbers?
faqs.answer: No. The pair loop requires left<right, so equal values need two distinct elements.

modules.title: Sliding Window
modules.description: Update contiguous ranges without recomputing every sum.

slides.title: A window contains a contiguous range
paragraphs: A subarray uses consecutive indices. A subsequence may skip positions. For [2,5,1], [2,5] is a subarray; [2,1] is only a subsequence. Sliding windows solve selected problems about contiguous ranges.

Represent a window as [left,right): left is included, right is excluded. Its length is right-left; [i,i) is empty. You will update a running sum as values enter and leave, then justify fixed-size and variable-size movement.
bullets: Maintain a contiguous half-open window
Reuse running sums
Prove when variable shrinking is safe

slides.title: Maximum sum of exactly k values
paragraphs: Add the value entering at right and advance right. If the window is longer than k, subtract the value leaving at left and advance left. Only compare against the best when the length equals k.
For [2,-1,4,3] with k=2, candidate sums are 1,3,7, so the answer is 7 starting at index 2. Updating by one addition and one subtraction avoids summing each k-element window from scratch.

slides.title: Negative values still work for fixed size
paragraphs: Fixed-size sum updates are arithmetic identities; they do not rely on values being nonnegative. For [-5,-2,-8] with k=2, the best sum is -7, not zero. Initialize the best from a real window, not an invented empty candidate.

Require integer k with 1≤k≤n. Empty input therefore has no valid fixed-size window and is rejected. k=1 chooses the greatest single value, and k=n chooses the whole array. Strict improvement keeps the earliest starting index when sums tie.

slides.title: Find the shortest window reaching a target
paragraphs: Here values must be nonnegative and target must be positive. Expand right until the running sum reaches the target. Record the current length, then remove values from the left while the sum still qualifies. This explores shorter qualifying windows ending at the same position.

For [2,3,1,2,4,3] and target 7, [4,3] has length 2. Empty input and a target larger than every possible window give no solution, represented by length 0. A length-0 window cannot meet a positive target.

slides.title: Nonnegative values justify shrinking
paragraphs: With nonnegative entries, adding a value cannot decrease the sum, and removing a value cannot increase it. Once removing the leftmost value makes the sum fall below target, further shrinking cannot repair that same window. Expansion is then necessary.

Left and right only advance. A zero may be removed without reducing the sum, which can still improve length. For [0,0,5] and target 5, shrink to the single value 5. The positive target prevents an empty qualifying window.

slides.title: The proof fails for unrestricted negatives
paragraphs: Consider [1,-1,5] with target 5. The whole window qualifies. Removing 1 drops the sum below target, but also removing -1 would raise the sum to 5 and reveal the shorter [5]. The nonnegative shrinking rule stops too early.

Therefore the selected variable-size algorithm rejects negative values. It does not silently drop them or apply an invalid proof. More general algorithms can solve signed-input variants, but they need different reasoning and are outside this lesson. Fixed-size maximum sum still accepts negatives.

slides.title: Incremental sums and monotone boundaries
paragraphs: In both algorithms, each value enters once and leaves at most once: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary state. A nested shrinking loop does not imply O(n²), because left advances at most n times over the entire run.

Use 64-bit sums in fixed-width examples. With at most 32 values of magnitude 100000, |sum|≤3200000, within exact JavaScript integer range as well. A result includes both the best sum/length and its starting position; window boundaries use the same half-open convention throughout.

faqs.question: Can a window skip a negative value?
faqs.answer: No. A window is contiguous. Skipping an interior element creates a subsequence, a different problem.

faqs.question: Why reject k=0?
faqs.answer: This lesson asks for exactly k actual elements and defines k in 1..n. An empty fixed window is outside that contract.

faqs.question: Why are negative values allowed in one example but not the other?
faqs.answer: Fixed-size sum updates always hold. The selected variable-size stopping proof needs nonnegative values.

faqs.question: Does the inner while loop make the variable example quadratic?
faqs.answer: No. Every left movement removes a new element; across the full run there are at most n such movements.

faqs.question: What does a best length of zero mean?
faqs.answer: No qualifying nonempty window was found, including on empty input. The positive target cannot be reached by an empty window.
